elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The abstract states the main objective/review question explicitly.

elements.quote: Editorials, commentaries, opinion papers, conference abstracts, media reports, letters, bulletins, pre-prints, grey literature, non-English language studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses were excluded from the search.
elements.reason: Exclusion criteria are specified in the abstract, but the main inclusion criteria are not stated there (only that 15 records met inclusion criteria).

elements.quote: a comprehensive search across PubMed and Embase databases was performed of peer-reviewed literature published from inception until June 2024
elements.reason: Information sources (PubMed, Embase) and the end date of the search (June 2024) are reported in the abstract.
The abstract does not mention any risk of bias or quality assessment methods; the ISPOR assessment appears only in the main text (text_8).
The abstract does not describe methods used to present or synthesize results (e.g., narrative synthesis is only reported in the main text, text_10).

elements.quote: The search yielded 2950 records, of which 15 met the inclusion criteria. The studies were carried out mainly in countries in Africa (53.3%)... The most used interventions for analyses were insecticide-treated bed nets (93.3%), IRS (80.0%)...
elements.reason: The abstract reports the number of included studies (15) and summarizes key study characteristics (geography, interventions, model types).

elements.quote: The methods used for estimating health benefits were compartmental models (40.0%), individual-based models (40.0%), static models (13.0%) and linear regression model (7%).
elements.reason: The abstract reports descriptive characteristics of included studies rather than results for the main outcomes (e.g., estimated health/cost benefits of interventions).

elements.quote: A narrative synthesis of the study characteristics was performed.
elements.reason: No meta-analysis was conducted; a narrative synthesis was performed, so no summary estimate applies.
No group comparisons with a direction of effect are reported; the review is a descriptive/narrative synthesis.
The abstract's conclusion does not summarize limitations of the included evidence such as risk of bias, inconsistency, or imprecision.

elements.quote: The findings highlighted the need for country-specific analysis for malaria control optimization... It is critical that the future modelling efforts account for fairness and target at risk malaria populations that are hard-to-reach to maximize impact.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results and their implications.
No funding source is stated in the abstract.

elements.quote: Trial registration : PROSPERO Registration number: CRD42023436966
elements.reason: The abstract section includes the register name (PROSPERO) and registration number.

elements.quote: Despite advances made in curbing the global malaria burden since the 2000s, progress has stalled, in part due to a plateauing of the financing available to implement needed interventions. In 2020, approximately 3.3 billion USD was invested globally for malaria interventions, falling short of the targeted 6.8 billion USD set by the GTS, increasing the financial gap between desirable and actual investment.
elements.reason: The abstract background describes the current state of knowledge (progress stalling, financing gap) but a dedicated Introduction section with a fuller account of existing knowledge and uncertainties was not retrieved.

elements.quote: Models for malaria control optimization are used to disentangle the most efficient interventions or packages of interventions for inherently constrained budgets. This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The need for the review is implied by the financing gap and the role of optimization models, but the rationale is only briefly stated in the abstract; no dedicated Introduction rationale text was retrieved.
No retrieved evidence discusses prior or existing systematic reviews on this topic or justifies an update/replication; the Introduction section was not available in the evidence.
Although the review covers interventions (ITNs, IRS, SMC, case management), no retrieved text describes a proposed mechanism of action for these interventions.
No retrieved evidence mentions a logic model or hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes.

elements.quote: The research question for this review was ' Are there English-language publications in peer-reviewed scientific journals describing how models have been used to allocate resources for malaria interventions in limited resource settings?' The main aim of this review was to identify and characterize models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in malaria control and elimination settings and to identify their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The review explicitly states both a research question and the main aim/objectives; the abstract (text_2) restates the aim: 'This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization... and assess their strengths and limitations.'

This is a review of optimization models for malaria resource allocation, not a review of intervention effects; no planned intervention comparisons are reported and PICO-style comparisons do not apply to the stated objectives.

elements.quote: Studies containing an optimization model (mathematical or statistical); (6) All studies with human Plasmodium species; (7) Studies with two or more interventions; (8) Cost data were used in combination with the model outputs; (9) Outcomes/health benefits were clearly stated and/or measured.
elements.reason: Inclusion criteria specify eligible study designs (optimization models), population (human Plasmodium, any subgroup), setting (any geographical region), interventions (two or more), and outcome requirements. No explicit follow-up requirement, but this is not essential for modelling studies.

elements.quote: (1) Were scientific peer-reviewed journals written in English; (2) Were published before 30th June 2024

elements.quote: The following records were excluded: (1) Editorials, commentaries, opinion papers, conference abstracts, media reports, letters, bulletins, pre-prints, grey literature; (2) Non-English language studies; (3) Systematic reviews, meta-analyses.
elements.reason: The review does not distinguish exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported; exclusion reasons listed are publication types, language, and review type only.

elements.quote: A narrative synthesis of the study characteristics was performed.

elements.quote: The findings highlighted the need for country-specific modelling analysis for malaria control optimization, country-specific epidemiological and cost data for analysis, performing cost sensitivity analyses and defining the perspective for the analysis, with an emphasis on subnational tailoring for data collection and analysis for more accurate and good quality results.
